title: I used AI as base for my animated sprites. Cats in Heat - Sunshine Resort [artoonu]
author: artoonu

comments.author: artoonu
comments.body:
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/2928950/Cats\_in\_Heat\_\_Sunshine\_Resort/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2928950/Cats_in_Heat__Sunshine_Resort/)

Adult-Only Casual Adventure game with animations, minigames, a funny story, and 3 cute catgirls!

comments.author: IriFlina
comments.body: What was your workflow? did you just cut up the parts in photoshop and animate it using live2d?

replies.author: artoonu
replies.body:
More or less. The idea is the same.

I cherry-picked a few generated outputs, photobashed and overpainted them, fixing errors and adding a touch of my style, I used Clip Studio Paint for that part.

Then I cut it up in pieces, rearranged those in Atlas Map, imported reference and Atlas to Blender, manually cut meshes, rigged, weight painted. And finally, animated.

I used this approach because Live2D has terrible SDK license and I was already familiar with Blender. Plus, it allows me to utilize the actual 3D features for better effect in some scenes.

replies.author: BlobbyMcBlobber
replies.body: Can you elaborate on the meshes you've created? Like how are the limbs connected? Do you use a skeleton?

replies.author: artoonu
replies.body:
Yes, skeleton, rig.

Each part (eg, forearm and upper arm) are separate meshes, overlapping points (joints) are overpainted on underneath part. In Blender3D I made a rig (skeleton) and bound the meshes to the bones, so that forearm bone affects both main part but also joint part of upper arm and upper arm bone, similarly, main area and joints of adjacent parts. That way, when moving limb, joints behave quite naturally. This process is called skinning or weight painting, where you assign which bones drives which vertices (mesh parts). The painting of overlaps I mentioned ensure there's no weird artifacts when bones are rotated too much.

In a few cases I mixed it with Shape Keys to fine-tune it, and connected it via driver bone so I have more control (for example you want to show elbow bone joint more).

comments.author: Bitterowner
comments.body: You would make a killing from mobile games, then go bigger once you got the funds.

replies.author: artoonu
replies.body:
It's the other way round, first you need funds to go mobile, and most money go towards advertising. You make a huge bet that either you get enough players so in-game ads make up for it or enough people get microtransactions. I've seen plenty of people jumping on mobile and ending in debt.

Mobile market is super harsh. I guess you meant a gacha-like or one of these dating sims. Those require a lot of design and continuous support. Making casual puzzles or something doesn't seem feasible, games are lost in the ocean of others and only one in a thousands gets lucky enough.
